title: Ask only for what can be done now
statement: Tie every instruction, hint and status line to the step the learner is on, never an earlier or hidden one, and ask only for what they can do now.
example: An independent visual review found 40 word-meaning cards whose status told students to explain the word before any box for explaining it was on screen.
detail: An audit of a Grade 3 and a Grade 5 reading course found three requests the screen could not meet. A lesson's opening rubric required tapping a line before the tapping control existed, a rehearsal page asked for a written plan with no box and no place named for it, and an independent visual review caught 40 word-meaning cards telling students to explain the word before the explanation step appeared. The repairs made the rubric ask for what a spoken or typed answer can supply, named a notebook for the plan and gave each card the instruction for its current stage. Earlier tests had never asked whether every instruction to produce something had a place to do it, and the course's published rules say every question on screen has an input.
against: The rubric case was found in source, not as a live grader rejection: 'No real grader rejection is established; the health response remains `ok:false`.' (`grade3-reading/ui-audit-2026-09-08/round-1/g3/PROPOSAL-REVIEW-by-unit9.md`, line 53). Other records let help point back: a-recap-of-the-worked-example lets students open a recap of what the worked example did, and point-only-at-steps-that-exist allows a line to point to another step as long as that step exists. Neither rule's effect on students was measured.
